The evolution of ConcurrentHashMap from Java 7 to Java 8 represents one of the most significant architectural shifts in the java.util.concurrent package, moving from coarse-grained segment locking to fine-grained bucket node locking combined with lock-free atomic operations. To understand this deep concurrency engineering problem, we must examine both implementations. In Java 7, ConcurrentHashMap was built around the Segment structure—a subclass of ReentrantLock. The hash map was divided into a fixed number of segments (by default 16), meaning that concurrent modifications could happen simultaneously only if they hashed to different segments. This reduced write contention compared to a globally locked Hashtable, but it suffered from memory overhead, unnecessary false contention if the segment count was configured too low, and linear traversal overhead inside long chains.

Java 8 completely abandoned the Segment architecture, aligning ConcurrentHashMap much closer to the modern layout of HashMap. It discarded ReentrantLock per segment and adopted a sophisticated mixture of Compare-And-Swap (CAS) primitives via Unsafe/VarHandles, synchronized blocks localized strictly to individual hash table bin heads (Node arrays), and treeification mechanics for high-collision scenarios. By lowering the synchronization granularity from an entire segment down to a single bucket node, Java 8 drastically increases throughput for concurrent puts and removes. Furthermore, it introduces advanced state-transfer mechanisms during resizing, allowing multiple worker threads to cooperatively transfer bins from the old table to the resized table, eliminating the single-thread bottleneck seen in older collections.

Dynamic, equal to the capacity of the underlying table bins
Singly linked lists per segment bucket
Singly linked lists transitioning to Red-Black Trees (TreeNode)
Single thread acquires segment lock and rehashes
Multi-threaded cooperative resizing via TransferNode markers

items: Java 7 Segment structure extends ReentrantLock, requiring explicit lock acquisition for every write operation, which consumes significant memory overhead due to object headers for every segment instance.

Java 8 utilizes Unsafe.compareAndSwapObject (or VarHandle in modern JDKs) to insert the first node into an empty bin lock-free, drastically cutting down CPU context switching under low-to-moderate contention.

When a hash collision occurs in Java 8, synchronization is acquired explicitly on the first node of the bin (synchronized(firstNode)) rather than locking an entire segment, allowing concurrent updates to other buckets in the same table.

Java 8 bin treeification converts linked lists exceeding TREEIFY_THRESHOLD (8) into Red-Black trees if table capacity is at least MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY (64), worst-case search dropping from O(N) to O(log N).

parsed_answer.content: A classic production anti-pattern in Java 8 ConcurrentHashMap is assuming that compound operations like check-then-act (e.g., if (map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v)) are atomic. Even though individual methods like put, get, and replace are thread-safe, composite logic requires atomic methods like putIfAbsent, compute, or merge. Additionally, be aware that during a resize operation in Java 8, traversing threads may encounter a ForwardingNode (hash code -1), which safely redirects read/write operations to the new underlying array.
